newsitem.title: FRANCE: Short campaign may boost French left -poll.
newsitem.headline: Short campaign may boost French left -poll.

text.p: The shortness of the campaign in France's snap parliamentary election will give a boost to candidates on the left, according to an opinion poll made public on Saturday.

The Ipsos poll for the weekly Marianne said this was because voters had so little time to learn about their local candidates that they were more likely to vote on the basis of their favourite national party in the May 25-June 1 election.

The left will reap the benefit because there is a smaller proportion of incumbents -- whose names are generally better known to voters than are challengers -- on the left in the outgoing National Assembly than the proportion of leftist voters in the population at large, Ipsos pollsters said.
The current centre-right majority, on the other hand, will suffer because it has a higher percentage of incumbents than its support in the population at large.
Ipsos said the combined left would get 43 percent of the vote based on national party preference compared to 39.5 percent if voters cast their ballots on the basis of the candidates' names.

Candidates from the current centre-right majority, on the other hand, would garner 35 percent of the vote on the basis of national party preference, compared to 38 percent if choices were made on the basis of candidates' names.
There was little or no difference in support for the other, smaller parties, the poll found.
The findings were based on a survey of 1,591 people aged 18 and over and conducted last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The poll found that few voters could name the candidates in their constituency or say what they stand for.
In addition, voters were unlikely to have enough time to learn more about them because the campaign is so short, the poll found.

Because of this, two out of three voters said they would vote on the basis of the various national parties' competing programmes and ideas, rather than on the qualifications of the individual candidates, according to the survey.
More than half of voters were unable to name even a single candidate in their own constituency, and 43 percent knew little or nothing about even the incumbent deputy.

The campaign is short because conservative President Jacques Chirac left just five weeks for campaigning when he announced on April 21 that he was dissolving parliament and calling an early National Assembly election for May 25, with a second run-off round of voting on June 1.
The election had initially been set for March 1998.
